summary: An announcement of a working meeting on the Telnet protocol, to be held at UCLA on March 5, 1973. Many changes and extensions had been proposed since RFC 318, and the aim was to agree on an official protocol with some room for optional features. Attendees were expected to have read a list of earlier RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: A call for people to meet and finally agree on the rules for connecting to faraway computers by typing, after lots of competing ideas.

subtitle: A 1973 call to standardize the Telnet remote login protocol

tldr.problem: The Telnet protocol remained unofficial and many proposals for changes and extensions had emerged since RFC 318, creating confusion in the community.
tldr.mechanism: A working meeting was convened at UCLA on March 5, 1973 to bring together experienced parties to hash out disagreements and define an official Telnet protocol with optional extensions.
tldr.outcome: This meeting marked a step toward standardizing Telnet, though the protocol would continue to evolve through subsequent RFCs.

today: RFC 461 is a historical record of the standardization effort for Telnet in early 1973. Telnet ultimately became an Internet Standard, defined in modern form by RFC 854 (protocol) and RFC 855 (options).

sections.title: The Telnet Standardization Challenge
sections.content: RFC 318 had proposed the TELNET protocol, but it remained unofficial. In the years following, the network community had submitted many proposals for changes and extensions, fragmenting the design. The goal was to reach consensus on an official protocol that could accommodate optional features and variations while keeping a common core.
sections.plainLanguage: People had lots of different ideas about how to let computers talk to each other through a keyboard. The network needed one official answer.

sections.title: The March 1973 Meeting
sections.content: Alex McKenzie announced a working meeting to be held at UCLA on Monday, March 5, 1973. The event was designed for serious technical participants who had already engaged with the protocol debates, not as a tutorial for newcomers. Attendees were expected to have read several prior RFCs on Telnet: RFCs 318, 328, 340, 357, 393, 426, and 435. McKenzie also noted that few (if any) actual hosts at the time followed the echo-control conventions described in RFC 318.
sections.plainLanguage: Alex McKenzie called a meeting at UCLA for people who already understood Telnet and the debates about it. They had to do their homework first.

sections.title: Defining an Official Protocol
sections.content: The meeting aimed to resolve the technical disagreements and reach consensus on an official Telnet protocol definition. This official version would have room for optional expansions and extensions, allowing experimentation while maintaining a standard baseline that all implementations could count on.
sections.plainLanguage: The goal was to write down one official set of rules, with some space built in for people to try new ideas.
